label: Tomato___Early_blight
description: A common fungal infection causing dark brown to black spots with concentric rings (target-board pattern) on older leaves. It spreads rapidly during warm, humid weather and causes premature leaf loss.
actionSteps: Prune and destroy infected lower leaves immediately to stop upward spore dispersal.
Apply protective copper-based fungicide or mancozeb early morning following product label instructions.
Switch strictly to drip irrigation or water root bases directly to keep foliage dry.
prevention: Maintain at least 50–60 cm plant spacing for adequate airflow.
Practice 3-year crop rotation avoiding other Solanaceae family members.
Apply clean organic straw mulch to stop fungal spores splashing from soil.

label: Tomato___Late_blight
description: A destructive water-mold disease producing pale green to water-soaked lesions that turn dark brown with fuzzy white fungal growth underneath. It can destroy an entire field within days during cool, rainy conditions.
actionSteps: Uproot and bury severely infected plants immediately outside the cultivation perimeter.
Spray recommended systemic fungicide following the product label and local agricultural extension advice.
Disinfect all pruning tools and stakes using a 10% bleach solution between rows.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seedlings and resistant cultivars recommended by the Department of Agriculture.
Ensure proper furrow drainage so monsoon rainwater discharges freely without ponding.
Scout crop daily during periods of high relative humidity (>90%) and cool night temperatures.

label: Tomato___Bacterial_spot
description: A bacterial disorder producing small, water-soaked, dark brown angular lesions on leaves with yellow halos. Warm temperatures and wind-driven rain accelerate bacterial transmission.
actionSteps: Do not enter or cultivate the crop while leaves are wet to prevent spreading the bacteria.
Apply copper bactericide mixed with mancozeb adhering to local extension guidelines.
Remove and safely burn or bury heavily spotted plant debris away from water channels.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds or hot-water treated seedlings.
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that damages leaf tissues and splashes bacteria.
Sterilize seedling nursery trays and handling tools before each planting cycle.

label: Tomato___Leaf_Mold
description: Fungal disease causing pale green to yellowish spots on upper leaf surfaces and velvety olive-green mold underneath. Thrives in humid poly-tunnels and dense enclosed canopies.
actionSteps: Increase row and plant ventilation by pruning non-productive suckers and lower foliage.
Apply approved protective fungicide covering both leaf undersides and upper surfaces.
Lower greenhouse or poly-tunnel humidity by opening side skirts during morning hours.
prevention: Select resistant hybrid tomato varieties for wet season cultivation.
Space rows sufficiently wide to ensure rapid drying of morning condensation.
Sanitize support strings, stakes, and greenhouse structures after each season.

label: Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot
description: Fungal leaf disease featuring numerous small, circular spots with dark brown margins and grey-white centres dotted with black specks. Leads to severe defoliation if left unchecked.
actionSteps: Strip off the lowest affected leaves as soon as initial spots appear.
Spray copper fungicide or chlorothalonil following the product label recommendations.
Do not cultivate or prune foliage during damp or rainy weather.
prevention: Eliminate solanaceous weed hosts (such as nightshades) around the field boundary.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops such as legumes, maize, or paddy for two seasons.
Mulch soil around plants with paddy straw to prevent spore splashing.

label: Tomato___Spider_mites_Two-spotted_spider_mite
description: Microscopic sap-sucking pests causing fine yellow stippling, bronzing, and delicate webbing across leaf undersides. Infestations explode rapidly during hot, dry weather spells.
actionSteps: Apply organic neem oil solution (5 ml/L) or insecticidal soap early morning.
Spray miticide or sulfur-based spray if infestation exceeds economic threshold.
Overhead misting in hot afternoons can suppress mite reproduction.
prevention: Keep field borders free of dry weeds and wild grass hosts.
Avoid excessive synthetic nitrogen fertilization which stimulates mite reproduction.
Conserve natural predatory mites and beneficial ladybird beetles.

label: Tomato___Target_Spot
description: Fungal infection creating brown circular lesions that expand with concentric rings, often resembling early blight. It thrives in high temperatures and prolonged leaf wetness.
actionSteps: Prune and destroy severely infected leaves and fallen fruit.
Apply broad-spectrum protectant fungicide adhering strictly to product label rates.
Improve air movement through the canopy with proper trellising and sucker pruning.
prevention: Ensure wide plant spacing and avoid excessive canopy density.
Do not rotate tomatoes with papaya, cucumber, or cotton which also host the fungus.
Use clean disease-free planting material from certified nurseries.

label: Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus
description: A viral disease transmitted by silverleaf whiteflies that results in upward curling, yellow leaf margins, and severe plant stunting. Infected young plants yield virtually no fruit.
actionSteps: Rogue out and incinerate infected plants immediately to protect neighbouring rows.
Install yellow sticky traps (15–20 per acre) at canopy level to trap adult whiteflies.
Spray bio-pesticide neem formulation or approved insecticide to control vector populations.
prevention: Erect 40-mesh fine insect-proof netting over seedling nursery beds.
Deploy silver or reflective plastic mulch to disorient incoming whiteflies.
Maintain a 4-week host-free fallow period between tomato and chilli crops.

label: Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus
description: A highly infectious virus that creates light and dark green mottled patterns, leaf distortion, and curled foliage. It spreads easily through mechanical contact, clothing, and pruning shears.
actionSteps: Remove and burn infected plants; never add them to compost piles.
Wash hands and dip tools into 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP) or skim milk before touching healthy plants.
Prohibit smoking or tobacco handling inside tomato fields to prevent transmission.
prevention: Plant certified virus-tested seeds or resistant cultivars.
Avoid handling seedlings unnecessarily during transplanting operations.
Sterilize seedling trays, support poles, and tools between crop cycles.

label: Tomato___healthy
description: Foliage exhibits vibrant deep green coloration, firm turgor pressure, uniform leaf morphology, and no visible lesions or insect infestation.
actionSteps: Continue regular irrigation maintaining uniform soil moisture.
Apply top-dressing fertilizer according to growth stage and soil test advice.
Scout the field weekly on both upper and lower leaf surfaces.
prevention: Maintain clean field perimeters and control wild weeds.
Ensure proper trellis support and ground clearance for lower branches.
Log periodic scans in AgroVision to monitor vegetative vigor.

label: Potato___Early_blight
description: A fungal infection causing dark brown angular spots with characteristic concentric rings on potato foliage. Symptoms typically initiate on mature lower canopy leaves.
actionSteps: Prune affected lower leaves where feasible without injuring the tuber mound.
Apply protective copper or mancozeb fungicide according to local extension dosage.
Irrigate early in the morning so sun and wind dry foliage quickly.
prevention: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops such as cabbage, carrot, or beans for two years.
Plant certified seed tubers treated with approved fungicide.
Ensure adequate potassium and balanced nitrogen to maintain plant vigor.

label: Potato___Late_blight
description: The most destructive potato disease, causing rapid blackening of foliage and white sporulation underneath during wet highland weather. Unchecked late blight rots both vine canopy and underground tubers.
actionSteps: Spray recommended systemic fungicide immediately upon the first forecast warning.
Cut and destroy haulms (potato foliage) 10 days before harvest to prevent tuber contamination.
Uproot and bury severely infected clusters away from the cultivation area.
prevention: Cultivate resistant varieties certified by Nuwara Eliya / Welimada research stations.
Build high, compact soil ridges around potato mounds to shield tubers from spore washdown.
Never store harvested tubers showing surface discolouration or soft wet rot.

label: Potato___healthy
description: Potato vines show uniform lush foliage with strong stems, upright posture, and absence of blight lesions, chlorosis, or insect feeding.
actionSteps: Maintain stable soil moisture especially during tuber initiation and swelling.
Ensure good hilling up of soil ridges to prevent greening of tubers.
Inspect plants weekly for cutworm and leafhopper activity.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed tubers.
Maintain proper field drainage channels to prevent waterlogging during monsoon.
Record routine scans in the app to monitor crop growth stage.

label: Pepper___Bacterial_spot
description: Bacterial infection causing small, circular, dark green water-soaked spots that turn dark brown with necrotic centres. Severe attacks trigger extensive leaf drop and blistered fruit spots.
actionSteps: Avoid all field work and pesticide applications while foliage is wet.
Apply approved copper-based bactericide in combination with mancozeb as advised by extension officers.
Remove infected plants showing severe stem or crown cankers.
prevention: Purchase certified seed or soak seed in hot water (50°C for 25 min) before nursery sowing.
Adopt drip irrigation or furrow watering in preference to overhead sprinkling.
Disinfect nursery trays, tools, and harvest crates with disinfectant solution.

label: Pepper___healthy
description: Leaves are glossy, dark green, and structurally sound with no curling, mottling, or spot lesions, indicating optimal chlorophyll density and crop vigor.
actionSteps: Maintain balanced watering at plant base to support continuous flowering and pod set.
Top dress with balanced NPK nutrients according to Department of Agriculture schedule.
Perform weekly scouting for thrips, mites, and aphids on tender new shoot tips.
prevention: Keep field borders clean of weeds that harbor thrips and viral vectors.
Apply organic mulch to retain root zone moisture and prevent soil erosion.
Track plant health using regular AgroVision diagnosis scans.

label: Chilli___Leaf_curl
description: Characterized by severe upward leaf curling, puckering, reduction of leaf blade area, and stunted shoots. Caused by thrips and whiteflies transmitting viral and mechanical stresses.
actionSteps: Rogue out and burn stunted, severely distorted plants early in the season.
Install yellow and blue sticky traps (20 per acre) above the crop canopy.
Apply neem extract or recommended organic insecticide targeting thrips and whiteflies.
prevention: Use 40-mesh nylon netting over seedling nursery beds.
Deploy reflective plastic mulch along planting beds to repel flying insect vectors.
Maintain crop-free barriers between consecutive solanaceous plantings.

label: Eggplant___healthy
description: Broad, vigorous velvety green leaves with thick stems and robust flowering. No signs of shoot borer damage, bacterial wilt, or leaf spots.
actionSteps: Ensure consistent deep watering during flowering and fruit development.
Top-dress with compost or organic manure every 3 weeks.
Inspect shoot tips for shoot and fruit borer boreholes.
prevention: Crop rotation with legumes or cereals.
Maintain adequate plant spacing (60 x 60 cm).
Regularly scout and record crop progress in the app.

label: General___Nitrogen_deficiency
description: General yellowing (chlorosis) beginning uniformly on older bottom leaves while veins remain slightly lighter. Causes thin, spindly stems and stunted vegetative development.
actionSteps: Apply balanced nitrogen fertilizer (Urea or Ammonium Sulfate) based on soil test rates.
Spray 1% foliar urea solution during early morning for rapid leaf absorption.
Incorporate well-rotted cattle manure or compost to restore soil organic reserves.
prevention: Conduct preseason soil testing to establish baseline fertility.
Split nitrogen top dressings across basal, vegetative, and flowering stages.
Avoid heavy waterlogging that leaches nitrogen out of the root zone.
